units.title: Convexity, optimality conditions and conditioning
outcomes: Prove the first- and second-order characterizations of a differentiable convex function on an open convex domain.
Distinguish stationary points, local minima and global minima, including degenerate Hessians.
Read smoothness, strong convexity and conditioning from a quadratic's eigenvalues.
units.why: An optimizer's behavior starts with the objective's geometry. These conditions tell you which local evidence certifies a global solution and which does not.

next.note: Apply curvature and conditioning to ridge regression.

study.title: EE364a: convex sets and convex functions
study.locator: Lecture 2 notes: Convex set (slide 2-3), Convex combination and convex hull (2-4), Hyperplanes and halfspaces (2-6), and Intersection (2-12)
study.depth: Read these headings only. Use the book below for the proofs; leave separation and generalized inequalities aside.

study.title: EE364a: derivative tests for convexity
study.locator: Lectures 3 and 4 notes: First-order condition (slide 3-7), Second-order conditions (3-8), and Examples (3-9): quadratic and least-squares functions

study.title: Convexity proofs and curvature bounds
study.depth: Prove the derivative tests using restrictions to lines. In 9.1.2 focus on the lower and upper quadratic models and the ratio M/m, not the width calculation.

focus: A convex set contains every segment between its points. A convex function has a convex domain and lies below each chord; its tangent planes lie below its graph.

For C2 functions on an open convex domain, a PSD Hessian everywhere characterizes convexity. At one stationary point, a PSD Hessian is only a necessary local-minimum condition; a PD Hessian is sufficient.
For f(x)=x'Qx/2 with symmetric positive definite Q, mu=lambda_min(Q), L=lambda_max(Q), and kappa=L/mu. The gradient is L-Lipschitz and the lower quadratic model uses mu/2.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, prove the first-order inequality in both directions, then prove the Hessian test by restricting to a segment. By hand use Q=diag(1,9): find grad f, mu=1, L=9, kappa=9 and f(1,1)=5. Check with NumPy float64 arrays, np.linalg.eigvalsh(Q) and np.linalg.cond(Q); scalar absolute differences from [1,9], 9 and 5 must be below 1e-12. No random draws are needed.
traps: Dropping the convex-domain assumption: 1/x^2 has positive second derivative on its disconnected domain, but that domain is not convex.
Calling every stationary point a minimum: x^2-y^2 has a saddle at the origin.
Equating strict and strong convexity: x^4 is strictly convex on R but has no positive global lower curvature bound.

selfTest.q: Where are the assumptions used in the first-order proof?
selfTest.a: Convexity of the domain keeps x+t(y-x) inside it. Convexity of f supplies the chord inequality; divide by positive t and use differentiability as t tends to zero. Conversely, apply the tangent inequality at z=theta*x+(1-theta)*y to x and y. Nonnegative weights preserve inequalities and cancel the derivative terms; domain convexity ensures z exists. At theta=0 or 1 the chord statement is equality.

selfTest.q: Why does a zero gradient certify a global minimum only in the convex case?
selfTest.a: The convex tangent lower bound becomes f(y)>=f(x) for every feasible y. Without convexity that lower bound need not hold; -x^2 has zero derivative at its maximum.

selfTest.q: Does a zero Hessian at a stationary point settle local optimality?
selfTest.a: No. At zero, x^4 has a minimum and -x^4 has a maximum; both have zero derivative and zero second derivative.

selfTest.q: Why is mu>0 needed for uniqueness?
selfTest.a: The strong-convexity midpoint inequality subtracts mu*||x-y||_2^2/8. Two distinct minimizers would therefore give a midpoint below the optimal value. Convexity keeps the midpoint feasible; mu>0 makes the subtraction strictly positive.

practice.name: Convex Optimization: Exercise 3.8, Second-order condition for convexity
practice.note: Attempt both directions before looking back at the first-order proof on p. 70. Give the disconnected-domain counterexample as well.

units.stopWhen: You can prove both derivative tests with their domain assumptions, classify the three stationary-point counterexamples, and recover the quadratic's curvature bounds without notes.

fit.note: Kept: EE364a and the book supply definitions, checkable proofs, quadratic geometry and a named proof exercise within five hours.

Derive unbiased minibatch gradients and their covariance under independent sampling with replacement.

next.note: Apply these update and state tests to neural-network training.

study.depth: Use the upper quadratic model to derive f(x-eta*g)<=f(x)-eta*(1-L*eta/2)*||g||_2^2. Distinguish this descent guarantee from the exact quadratic contraction below.

study.title: GD, stochastic updates and minibatch noise
study.locator: Sections 12.3.1 to 12.3.2 (Gradient Descent), 12.4.1 to 12.4.2 (Stochastic Gradient Descent), and 12.5.2 (Minibatches)
study.depth: Follow the adjacent GD and minibatch pages. Use the PyTorch tab for update cells only; skip datasets, training loops and timing claims.

study.title: Heavy-ball dynamics on quadratics
study.locator: Sections 12.6.1.2 to 12.6.1.4 and 12.6.3.1 to 12.6.3.2; PyTorch momentum_2d cell

focus: In the eigenbasis, GD errors obey e_{k+1,i}=(1-eta*lambda_i)e_{k,i}. Uniform convergence for all starts requires 0<eta<2/L; eta=2/(L+mu) minimizes the worst factor to (kappa-1)/(kappa+1).
Heavy-ball uses x_{k+1}=x_k-eta*grad f(x_k)+beta*(x_k-x_{k-1}). Each eigenmode has characteristic polynomial r^2-(1+beta-eta*lambda)r+beta; repeated roots can produce a transient k*r^k factor.

For f=(1/n)sum f_i and independent uniform indices, the minibatch average gradient is unbiased and has covariance Sigma/B. Sampling without replacement has a finite-population correction; reshuffling is not independent sampling.
On a general L-smooth lower-bounded objective, the descent lemma controls objective decrease, not global optimality. Report full-objective residuals separately from noisy minibatch gradients.
units.reproduce: By hand derive the GD eigenmode recurrence and heavy-ball polynomial. In NumPy float64 use Q=diag(1,9), x0=(1,1), x_{-1}=x0. After ten updates, GD with eta=0.2 has ||x10||_2=0.151850025 and ||x10||_2/||x0||_2=0.1073741824=0.8^10 in exact arithmetic (measured absolute discrepancy 1.4e-17, allow 1e-12). Heavy-ball with eta=0.25 and beta=0.25 has ||x10||_2=0.0166875073. At eta=2/9 GD's second coordinate alternates without shrinking; at eta=0.23 its magnitude after ten steps is 1.96715136. Then create rng=np.random.default_rng(5); make its only draw noise=rng.standard_normal((10000,4),dtype=np.float64), in array row order. np.var(noise[:,0],ddof=1) is 0.984311 and np.var(noise.mean(axis=1),ddof=1) is 0.251557. Derive the theoretical variances 1 and 1/4; these measured values are not exact theoretical equalities. Allow absolute 1e-6 for the displayed simulation values.
traps: Including 2/L in the convergent interval. The largest-curvature mode has multiplier -1 there.
Claiming momentum contracts by its asymptotic spectral radius at every step. Repeated roots and initial state affect transients.
Calling the squared-gradient moment a noise variance, or assuming four correlated gradients reduce variance by four. Independence matters.

selfTest.q: Why is the quadratic rate a Euclidean error rate, not the same objective-gap rate?
selfTest.a: Symmetry gives an orthonormal eigenbasis; positivity gives eigenvalues in [mu,L]. Every error multiplier has magnitude at most rho, hence ||e_k||_2<=rho^k||e_0||_2, including the base case k=0. The quadratic gap weights squared errors, so it contracts by at most rho^(2k).

selfTest.q: What happens at eta=2/L if the initial error has no largest-eigenvalue component?
selfTest.a: It may still converge in the remaining modes. The strict bound guarantees convergence for every initial error, rather than claiming every start fails at the boundary.

selfTest.q: Why does minibatch covariance divide by B?
selfTest.a: Center each gradient and expand the covariance of their average. Independence makes cross-covariances zero; identical sampling gives B diagonal terms Sigma, divided by B^2. Unbiasedness follows from uniform sampling of the average objective.

selfTest.q: Does constant-step SGD converge exactly when additive gradient noise persists?
selfTest.a: Generally no. For scalar curvature lambda, independent zero-mean noise variance sigma^2 and |1-eta*lambda|<1 give limiting error variance eta*sigma^2/(lambda*(2-eta*lambda)). The variance recurrence adds eta^2*sigma^2 at every step.

practice.name: D2L: momentum on multiple eigenvalues
practice.locator: Section 12.6.5, Exercise 2: f(x)=sum lambda_i*x_i^2/2, lambda_i=2^(-i), x_i=1

study.depth: Read the schedule formulas and run the PyTorch learning-rate assignment and scheduler definitions only. Skip Fashion-MNIST training. Define whether your clock counts updates or epochs.

study.title: Decoupled decay and optimizer state
study.locator: AdamW algorithm box, eps and weight_decay parameters, state_dict and load_state_dict

study.title: Gradient-norm clipping contract
study.locator: clip_grad_norm_: concatenated-gradient norm, in-place modification, max_norm, norm_type and error_if_nonfinite

focus: With m0=0, m_t=(1-beta1)sum_{i=1}^t beta1^(t-i)*g_i. Constant E[g_i]=gbar gives E[m_t]=(1-beta1^t)*gbar; constant E[g_i^2] gives the analogous second-moment correction. Independence is not needed for these expectations.
Correction normalizes the finite weights. It does not make mhat/sqrt(vhat) an unbiased gradient estimate when gradients change or the denominator is random.

Clipping projects g onto a Euclidean ball: g*min(1,c/||g||_2), with zero mapped to zero. Clip before updating moments. AdamW shrinks parameters separately; adding lambda*theta to g changes both moments instead.

A schedule needs a clock and restart state. A small step caused by a tiny learning rate is not evidence of stationarity; check the un-clipped full-objective gradient and use the residual unit's stopping contract.
units.reproduce: Derive the finite-sum correction by induction, checking t=1. For constant g=(2,-1), beta1=0.9 and beta2=0.999, hand-compute m3=(0.542,-0.271) and v3=(0.011988004,0.002997001); corrected moments are (2,-1) and (4,1) in exact arithmetic. Check in NumPy float64 with infinity-norm tolerance 1e-12. Then run ten float64 updates on f(theta)=(theta1^2+9*theta2^2)/2 from (1,-2), m0=v0=0, epsilon=1e-6, decay=0.1, lr_t=0.01/(1+0.1*(t-1)), t=1,...,10. Clip g to Euclidean norm 1 using the exact formula above; update moments, then theta=(1-lr_t*0.1)*theta-lr_t*mhat/(sqrt(vhat)+epsilon). Result: (0.92127176,-1.91402438), allowing 1e-8 in infinity norm for the displayed rounding. Compare torch.optim.AdamW on CPU with float64, the same clipped gradients, betas=(0.9,0.999), eps=1e-6, weight_decay=0.1, foreach=False and the same per-update lr. On PyTorch 2.14.1 the measured infinity-norm difference is 2.22e-16; allow 1e-12. Do not substitute clip_grad_norm_ in this oracle comparison, because its stabilizing denominator changes the mathematical projection slightly. Save theta,m,v,t and the schedule clock after step five and check resumed versus uninterrupted final states within 1e-12. No random draws are needed.
traps: Starting the bias-correction clock at zero, or incrementing it once per coordinate instead of once per update.
Putting epsilon inside the square root while claiming the Adam formula with epsilon outside it.
Restoring parameters but not moments and the schedule clock. The next update is then a different algorithmic state.

selfTest.q: What assumptions does the bias-correction derivation actually use?
selfTest.a: Zero initial moments remove a beta^t*m0 term. Constant beta in [0,1) supplies the finite geometric sum and a nonzero denominator for t>=1. Equal first or second moments of the gradient sequence let expectation factor out of the weighted sum. Independence is not required.

selfTest.q: Why is Adam's vhat not the gradient variance?
selfTest.a: It estimates an uncentered second moment. Variance subtracts the square of the mean; vhat does not.

selfTest.q: When does coupled L2 match decoupled decay?
selfTest.a: For plain SGD with no momentum or preconditioner, theta-eta*(g+lambda*theta) equals (1-eta*lambda)*theta-eta*g in exact arithmetic. Adaptive scaling or momentum generally destroys this equivalence.

selfTest.q: What is the norm-clipping solution for g=(3,4) and c=2?
selfTest.a: Its norm is 5, so the projection is (1.2,1.6). Clamping each coordinate to [-2,2] gives (2,2), which is a different projection and exceeds norm 2.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: implement adaptive updates, clipping and update-indexed schedules; test finite-sum moments, checkpoint/resume and an un-clipped stationarity residual on the same deterministic quadratic.
units.stopWhen: You can derive the correction with its assumptions and pass moment, decay-placement and restart tests, including the 1e-12 infinity-norm oracle comparison.

study.title: Lagrangian lower bounds and KKT certificates
study.depth: Stop 5.5.3 after Example 5.1 on p. 244. Keep only the duality needed to explain weak duality, Slater's condition and the small QP; leave broader duality theory aside.

study.locator: Changing the problem, Infeasible and unbounded problems, and Other problem statuses
study.depth: Use the solver only after deriving the analytic solution. Accept neither optimal_inaccurate nor an iteration cap as an unchecked certificate.

study.title: Proximal maps, soft thresholding and lasso
study.depth: In 4.2 read the basic update and quadratic upper-model interpretation. Skip accelerated methods and ADMM. In 6.5.2 stop before projection onto the l1 ball.

focus: Write inequalities as f_i(x)<=0 and attach nonnegative multipliers. The dual function minimizes the Lagrangian over x without imposing the original constraints; weak duality gives a lower bound.

KKT comprises primal feasibility, dual feasibility, stationarity and complementary slackness. For a differentiable convex problem with affine equalities, KKT is sufficient; Slater's condition supplies necessity and dual attainment when a primal optimum exists.
For 0.5*||Aw-b||_2^2+lambda*||w||_1, proximal gradient takes u=w-eta*A'(Aw-b), then w+=sign(u)*max(|u|-eta*lambda,0). The threshold scales with eta, not just lambda.

At zero, the l1 subgradient is the interval [-1,1]. Derive the three scalar cases instead of pretending abs has a unique derivative there. For the smooth part, eta<=1/||A||_2^2 gives the quadratic upper-model descent argument.
units.reproduce: By hand minimize 0.5*||x-a||_2^2 with a=(2,-1), x>=0 and x1+x2=1. Use L=0.5*||x-a||_2^2-lambda'x+nu*(sum(x)-1). Obtain x*=(1,0), lambda*=(0,2), nu*=1 and primal value 1. Derive g(lambda,nu)=0.5*||a||_2^2-0.5*||a+lambda-nu*1||_2^2-nu; its value at the certificate is 1. In CVXPY 1.9.3 use float64 a, z=cp.Variable(2), constraints=[z>=0,cp.sum(z)==1], objective=cp.Minimize(0.5*cp.sum_squares(z-a)); solve with solver='CLARABEL', tol_gap_abs=tol_gap_rel=tol_feas=1e-10, max_iter=100. Read lambda=constraints[0].dual_value and nu=constraints[1].dual_value. Status is optimal. Measured residuals: max(0,max(-z))=8.08e-13, abs(sum(z)-1)=1.11e-16, max(0,max(-lambda))=0, ||z-a-lambda+nu||_inf=1.22e-11 and ||lambda*z||_inf=4.56e-11. ||z-(1,0)||_inf=8.08e-13. Require every residual and the solution difference <=1e-9, rather than exact feasibility. Then derive the scalar soft-threshold map and work A=I2, b=(2,-0.25), lambda=0.5 by hand: w*=(1.5,0). From w0=(0,0), take 30 NumPy float64 proximal steps with eta=0.5; the infinity-norm error against this closed form is 1.40e-9, allowed <=2e-9. No random draws are needed.
traps: Giving x>=0 the wrong multiplier sign. Its standard-form constraint is -x<=0, so stationarity contains -lambda.
Inferring a positive multiplier from an active constraint. Complementary slackness only says a positive multiplier implies activity, not the converse.
Using ridge's shrinkage as lasso's proximal operator. Ridge scales coordinates continuously; lasso thresholds a whole interval to zero.

selfTest.q: Where does each assumption enter the KKT sufficiency proof?
selfTest.a: Convex objective and inequality functions, affine equalities, and nonnegative multipliers make L convex in x. Differentiability and stationarity therefore minimize L globally. Feasibility and complementary slackness make L(x*)=f(x*). The dual infimum is then f(x*), so weak duality certifies optimality. Slater is not needed for sufficiency.

selfTest.q: Does this QP satisfy Slater's condition?
selfTest.a: Yes. x=(0.5,0.5) strictly satisfies -x<0 and satisfies the affine equality. This supplies the constraint qualification; the strictly convex objective also makes the primal optimizer unique.

selfTest.q: Why is the proximal minimizer zero when |u|<=eta*lambda?
selfTest.a: At w=0 the stationarity inclusion is 0 in -u+eta*lambda*[-1,1], exactly that inequality. The quadratic term is strictly convex, so this condition identifies the unique minimizer, including both threshold endpoints.

selfTest.q: How can you check a lasso answer without knowing w*?
selfTest.a: Let h=A'(Aw-b). Nonzero coordinates need h_i+lambda*sign(w_i)=0; zero coordinates need |h_i|<=lambda. Check these residuals with a stated numerical zero threshold, or use ||w-S_{eta*lambda}(w-eta*h)||/eta as a proximal-gradient residual.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: derive and solve a changed two-coordinate QP, record all KKT residuals and solver status, and derive soft thresholding before checking a lasso proximal loop against a closed form and a solver oracle.
units.stopWhen: You can derive the QP certificate and threshold endpoints unaided, and your NumPy and solver checks pass their stated infinity-norm and feasibility tolerances.

fit.note: Coverage failed for a proximal-gradient lasso derivation. Parikh and Boyd fill that gap; the pool's duality chapter and CVXPY remain the KKT route, with practice specified for the mini-project.

study.locator: Sections 9.5.1 to 9.5.3 (pp. 484 to 491), and the Summary on p. 496
study.depth: Read the step, decrement and proof assumptions; follow the quadratically convergent phase argument on pp. 490 to 491. Skip 9.5.4's large numerical examples and 9.6.

study.title: Newton as rootfinding
study.locator: Section 4.3.1, equations 4.3.3 to 4.3.8, and Section 4.3.2's newton algorithm
study.depth: Apply the rootfinding argument to the objective's derivative. Inspect the stopping conditions rather than treating small successive steps as a certificate.

study.title: A quasi-Newton comparison with an analytic gradient
study.locator: BFGS method; options gtol, maxiter, c1, c2 and hess_inv0; Notes on precision loss
study.depth: Use the default line-search parameters and initial inverse-Hessian approximation. Do not study or implement a full BFGS convergence proof here.

focus: Minimizing the local quadratic model gives H*p=-g. Solve this system instead of forming H^{-1}. Positive definite H makes g'p<0 for nonzero g; an indefinite Hessian does not.

A Lipschitz Hessian and a uniformly bounded inverse Hessian near a nondegenerate minimizer give a quadratic error bound for full Newton steps, once the starting point is close enough. Backtracking handles the approach to that neighborhood.

Quasi-Newton methods replace freshly evaluated curvature with an approximation informed by gradient changes. Their iteration count alone hides line-search evaluations; BFGS is an oracle here, not a second implementation assignment.
units.reproduce: By hand minimize phi(x)=x^4/4+x^2/2-2x on R. Its gradient is x^3+x-2, Hessian 3x^2+1, and unique minimizer x*=1. Derive Newton's update and the exact recurrence e_next=e^2*(2*x+1)/(3*x^2+1), where e=x-1. Starting at x0=1.5, use NumPy float64 for four updates: absolute errors after each are 0.1290322581, 0.01124439868, 9.394478985e-5 and 6.618699366e-9. Compare each displayed error with absolute tolerance 1e-10. The first four ratios |e_next|/e^2 are 0.516129, 0.675367, 0.743020 and 0.749941, approaching 3/4; stop the rate measurement before rounding dominates. With SciPy 1.18.1, call minimize on the same scalar objective with x0=np.array([1.5],dtype=np.float64), jac returning np.array([x[0]**3+x[0]-2],dtype=np.float64), method='BFGS', options={'gtol':1e-10,'maxiter':100}. It reports success, eight iterations, nine function and nine gradient evaluations, and gradient infinity norm 1.32e-13. Require |x-1|<=1e-9 and ||grad||_inf<=1e-10; compare work at that residual, counting Newton's derivative and Hessian calls too. Do not infer a timing advantage. No random draws are needed.
traps: Applying the rootfinding Newton formula to phi rather than phi'. That finds a zero of the loss, not its stationary point.
Claiming quadratic convergence at a multiple root, or from every starting point. A vanishing derivative breaks the local denominator bound.
Counting BFGS iterations while ignoring its line-search calls, or interpreting solver success without checking the returned gradient.

selfTest.q: Why does this example converge to 1 from 1.5?
selfTest.a: For x>1, the recurrence gives e_next>0. Also e_next/e=(x-1)*(2x+1)/(3x^2+1)<1 because the denominator minus the numerator is x^2+x+2>0. The iterates decrease and stay above 1; their limit must solve x^3+x-2=0. Positive Hessian makes that root unique. Dividing the recurrence by e^2 gives the limit 3/4.

selfTest.q: Where are the local Newton proof assumptions used?
selfTest.a: A Lipschitz Hessian bounds the Taylor remainder by a constant times ||e||_2^2. Nonsingularity and local inverse bounds keep solving with H from amplifying it without limit. A sufficiently close start keeps the iterates in that neighborhood; full steps give the Newton error cancellation.

selfTest.q: What happens to Newton rootfinding for F(x)=(x-r)^2?
selfTest.a: For x!=r the update is x_next=x-(x-r)/2, so e_next=e/2: linear, not quadratic. The simple-root assumption fails because F'(r)=0.

selfTest.q: Must a Newton direction descend at a stationary saddle?
selfTest.a: No. At a stationary point g=0, the Newton step is zero when the Hessian is invertible, even if the point is a saddle. Away from it, an indefinite Hessian can also give a non-descent direction.

study.title: Inspect low-precision formats
study.locator: torch.finfo: bits, eps, max, tiny, smallest_normal and the note about subnormal numbers

focus: With p total significand bits including the hidden leading one, spacing in [2^e,2^(e+1)) is 2^(e-(p-1)). eps is the gap above 1; unit roundoff for round-to-nearest is eps/2. The relative bound needs normal-range results and no overflow.
float64, float32, float16 and bfloat16 have p=53,24,11,8 and exponent fields of 11,8,5,8 bits respectively. bfloat16 has wide range but coarser spacing than float16.
Overflow produces infinities; gradual underflow first reaches subnormals with reduced relative precision. tiny is the smallest positive normal, not the smallest positive representable value.

Subtracting nearby rounded operands can destroy relative accuracy even when the subtraction itself is exact. Separate conditioning of the requested difference from avoidable instability in how its operands were formed.
units.reproduce: By hand enumerate the d=4 fractional-bit system in FNC Exercise 1.1.1 and derive its spacing. Then use np.finfo for np.float64, np.float32 and np.float16, and torch.finfo(torch.bfloat16) on CPU for bfloat16. Print eps, tiny and max to three significant digits: float64 (2.22e-16,2.23e-308,1.80e308), float32 (1.19e-7,1.18e-38,3.40e38), float16 (9.77e-4,6.10e-5,6.55e4), bfloat16 (7.81e-3,1.18e-38,3.39e38). Derive eps=2^(-(p-1)) and check each eps within relative scalar tolerance 1e-6. Inspect np.nextafter(dtype(0),dtype(1)), and torch.nextafter on CPU bfloat16 scalars, to see values below tiny. In NumPy float64 set x=np.float64(1e8): sqrt(x*x+1)-x returns 0, while 1/(sqrt(x*x+1)+x) returns about 5.00e-9. Rationalize the expression by hand and bound the exact result's difference from 1/(2*x) by 1/(8*x^3); allow absolute 1e-20 for the stable scalar. Finally evaluate np.exp(np.float64(1000)) and np.exp(np.float64(-1000)) inside np.errstate(over='ignore',under='ignore'): outputs are inf and 0. These are range failures, not exact evaluations of exp. No random draws are needed.
traps: Calling eps the smallest representable number, or calling finfo.tiny the smallest subnormal.
Assuming bfloat16 is more precise because its exponent range is larger.
Applying a relative error tolerance at a true zero, or claiming that a stable rewrite recovers information already rounded out of its inputs.

selfTest.q: Why is round-to-nearest error bounded by eps/2 in the normal range?
selfTest.a: In each binade the absolute error is at most half its spacing. Dividing by |x|>=2^e bounds relative error by 2^(-(p-1))/2. The lower bound on |x| uses normal binade representation; subnormals instead have fixed absolute spacing. Overflow is excluded.

selfTest.q: What is lost in sqrt(x*x+1)-x at x=1e8?
selfTest.a: x*x is about 1e16, where float64 spacing is 2, so adding 1 rounds away under ties-to-even. The square root returns x and subtraction gives zero. Rationalization avoids subtracting nearly equal operands; it does not make x*x+1 exact.

selfTest.q: Is the computed zero an underflow of the true answer?
selfTest.a: No. The true answer is about 5e-9, well within the normal float64 range. It is cancellation after an earlier rounding loss.

selfTest.q: Can (1+eps/2)-1 and 1+(eps/2-1) differ in float64?
selfTest.a: Yes. Under round-to-nearest ties-to-even, the first evaluates to zero and the second to about 1.11e-16. The real-arithmetic associative law does not transfer to rounded operations.
